name: Bretag's 5 Core Elements of Exemplary AI Policy
author: Tracey Bretag
source: Bretag et al. (2011) IJEI 7(2):3-12 — analysis of all 40 Australian university policies
dinh_nghia: Bretag et al. (2011) identified five core elements that characterize exemplary academic integrity policies, derived from a systematic analysis of all 40 Australian university academic integrity policies. The framework — often called the AARDS framework or '5 Core Elements' — specifies what makes a policy effective at promoting integrity rather than merely punishing violations. The five elements are: Access (policy is accessible and communicated to all stakeholders), Approach (proactive, educative stance rather than purely punitive), Responsibility (shared — students, faculty, and institutions all bear responsibility), Detail (clear, specific definitions and procedures), and Support (resources and support structures accompany the policy). Though originally developed for academic integrity broadly, the framework is directly applicable to AI-era policy design.
phan_loai: Bretag's framework is an evaluative/prescriptive meta-framework for policy quality rather than a violation taxonomy. Policy failures can be diagnosed through missing elements: (1) Access failure — policy exists but students/faculty are unaware of it; (2) Approach failure — policy is purely punitive with no educational component; (3) Responsibility failure — only students are held accountable, not the institution or faculty who designed AI-vulnerable assessments; (4) Detail failure — policy does not define what AI use is prohibited or permitted in specific contexts; (5) Support failure — no AI literacy training, no advising resources, no appeals process. AI-era policies that prohibit AI but provide no AI literacy support fail the Approach and Support elements.
lich_su_khai_niem: The 5 Core Elements framework was published in the International Journal for Educational Integrity in 2011 (IJEI 7(2):3-12). Bretag led a research project auditing all 40 Australian university academic integrity policies — producing the most comprehensive empirical foundation for what effective policies contain. The framework predates widespread AI awareness but has proven remarkably prescient: every element it identifies is violated by the wave of reactive AI prohibition policies issued in 2023-2024. Bretag extended this work in the 'Handbook of Academic Integrity' (Springer, 2016), the authoritative academic integrity reference.
ten_truong_hop: The 5 Core Elements framework has been applied to policy audit in Australia, UK, Canada, and internationally. Direct applications: Australian government higher education reviews cited Bretag's elements; UK QAA academic integrity guidance (2023) aligns with the framework; multiple Canadian university policy reviews reference Bretag et al. (2011). The framework was also applied to analyze institutional AI policies in 2023-2024, finding that most reactive AI prohibition policies failed on the Approach and Support elements.
dien_bien: Bretag's methodology: collected all 40 Australian university academic integrity policies, developed a coding framework based on policy science literature, identified patterns across policies, and inductively derived the 5 elements that distinguished exemplary from inadequate policies. Key finding: most policies at the time were detailed on violations and punishments (Detail — procedures) but weak on educational approach, shared responsibility, and student support. The framework was subsequently validated across multiple national contexts.
ket_qua_xu_ly: The 5 Core Elements framework became the standard for academic integrity policy audit internationally. Bretag's Handbook of Academic Integrity (2016) is the most-cited reference work in the field. The framework has been used by higher education regulatory bodies in Australia, UK, and Canada as a quality benchmark. In the AI era, researchers applying Bretag's framework to university AI policies (2023-2024) consistently found deficiencies in the Approach element (educational support) and the Responsibility element (institutional vs. student accountability).
con_so_thong_ke: Based on analysis of 40 Australian university policies; published 2011 IJEI 7(2):3-12; 5 elements; framework has been applied in policy audits across Australia, UK, Canada [uncertain: exact count of institutional applications]; Bretag's Handbook (2016) is one of the most cited works in academic integrity research with 500+ citations [uncertain: exact citation count].
hai_cho_nguoi_hoc: Bretag's Responsibility element specifically identifies shared responsibility: students are harmed when institutions hold them solely accountable for integrity violations while the institution designs AI-vulnerable assessments and provides no AI literacy training. The Support element ensures students have resources to act with integrity — when support is absent, students face integrity challenges without institutional scaffolding.
hai_cho_nghien_cuu: The Detail element requires policies to clearly define what counts as a violation in research contexts — including AI-assisted writing, hallucinated citations, and undisclosed AI use. Without detail, researchers face ambiguity about permissible AI assistance in manuscript preparation, data analysis, and literature review — leading to inconsistent enforcement that undermines research integrity norms.
hai_cho_xa_hoi: Weak policies (failing Bretag's elements) produce credential inflation without genuine competency assurance. The Access element ensures all students know the rules — without access, enforcement is inequitable (penalizing students unaware of policies). The Approach element protects educational value: punitive-only approaches push violations underground rather than building genuine integrity.
cong_cu_phat_hien: Bretag's framework does not address detection tools directly (2011 predates AI detectors). However, the Detail element requires policies to specify how violations are detected and adjudicated. The Approach element cautions against over-reliance on surveillance and detection at the expense of education — directly relevant to the Turnitin/GPTZero debate. An exemplary policy specifies detection tools, their limitations, and the evidentiary standards for using detector output in disciplinary proceedings.
han_che_cong_cu: The Approach and Support elements are most relevant to detection tool limitations. An exemplary AI integrity policy (meeting Bretag's standards) would: (1) Specify detection tools as one input, not definitive evidence; (2) Include ESL/EAL student support to reduce false-positive risk; (3) Provide faculty training on detection tool limitations (Liang et al., 2023); (4) Establish a support pathway for students wrongly accused by AI detectors.
watermarking: LLM watermarking would satisfy Bretag's Detail element if policies specify it as an integrity mechanism. However, the Approach element requires educational rather than purely surveillance-based solutions — watermarking is a detection technology, not an educational intervention. An exemplary policy combining watermarking with AI literacy education would better satisfy all 5 elements.
thiet_ke_bai_tap: Bretag's framework applies to assessment design through the Responsibility element: institutions that design AI-vulnerable assessments (generic essay prompts, low-stakes take-home work) share responsibility for the violations they invite. Exemplary policy (meeting the Detail element) specifies assessment-level expectations — what AI use is permissible in each task type. This directly motivates AIAS-like tiered assessment design.
chinh_sach_truong_hoc: The 5 Core Elements are the de facto standard for academic integrity policy quality. Applied to major AI policies: Stanford's contextual AI use policy meets Access and Detail but is weak on institutional Responsibility (it focuses on student obligations). NUS's disclosure framework meets Approach (educative) and Support (training provided) but Detail varies by faculty. Bretag's framework reveals that no university has yet produced a fully exemplary AI integrity policy meeting all 5 elements consistently.
van_hoa_to_chuc: The Approach element is Bretag's most direct contribution to organizational culture theory: effective policies are proactive and educational, not purely punitive. This aligns with McCabe's finding that honor code cultures outperform enforcement-only cultures. Bretag provides the policy-level mechanism: institutional policies must embody an educative approach to produce integrity culture, not just integrity compliance.
ai_literacy: The Support element directly requires AI literacy resources as part of any exemplary AI integrity policy. Students must have access to training on what AI tools do, when use is appropriate, and how to attribute AI contributions. An AI integrity policy that prohibits AI without providing AI literacy support fails the Support element. This aligns with UNESCO 2023 guidance and EU AI Act Article 4.
khung_quoc_te: Bretag's 5 Core Elements are the policy quality standard that UNESCO 2023, EU AI Act, and ICAI guidance implicitly require. UNESCO 2023's recommendation to support students in using AI 'effectively, ethically and transparently' maps to Approach + Support. EU AI Act Article 4 (AI literacy) maps to Support. ICAI's 6 values provide the normative content; Bretag's elements provide the policy architecture. The frameworks are complementary at different levels of analysis.
phap_luat_viet_nam: Vietnam's Decree 109/2022 Dieu 20 fails at least 3 of Bretag's 5 elements when applied to AI integrity: (1) Access — no specific AI guidance communicated to students; (2) Approach — purely punitive framing; (3) Support — no AI literacy training mandated. The Bretag framework provides a diagnostic tool for MOET to assess and improve Vietnam's academic integrity regulatory framework. A Bretag-compliant Vietnamese AI integrity policy would require cross-ministry coordination (MOET + MOST) for the Support element.
chinh_sach_chau_a: Asian institutional AI policies analyzed through Bretag's elements: CUHK 2023 prohibition policy — Detail (clear prohibition) but weak on Approach (punitive) and Support (no AI literacy mandate); NUS disclosure framework — strong on Approach and Support, adequate on Detail; NTU zero-marks policy — Detail (specific consequence) but weak on Support. The Bretag framework explains why NUS's approach is more sustainable than CUHK's or NTU's: it satisfies more of the 5 elements.
ai_tutor_vs_ai_cheater: Bretag's framework reframes the tutor/cheater debate as a policy design question: an institution with an exemplary policy (meeting all 5 elements) creates conditions where AI can legitimately function as a tutor (because students understand appropriate use through Access and Support) and cannot easily function as a cheater (because policies Detail specific prohibitions with educational Approach). The dichotomy dissolves under good policy design.
edtech_company_policies: Bretag's Support element requires that EdTech platforms used in academic contexts provide integrity-promoting features. Khan Academy Khanmigo's Socratic design supports the Approach element (educative rather than enabling). Turnitin's integration with educational feedback tools attempts to meet Approach. However, most AI writing tools (ChatGPT, Gemini, Copilot) provide no academic integrity support features — violating what Bretag's Support element would require of institutional policies governing their use.
de_xuat_nha_nghien_cuu: Applying Bretag's framework to EdTech AI integrity research: (1) Use the 5 Core Elements as an audit instrument to evaluate university AI policies systematically; (2) Recommend that Vietnamese universities audit their Decree 109 compliance against Bretag's elements; (3) Prioritize the Support element in Vietnamese policy development — AI literacy is the most actionable reform; (4) The Responsibility element provides the theoretical basis for arguing that universities (not only students) bear accountability for AI-enabled academic fraud when assessment design is AI-vulnerable; (5) Publish a Bretag-framework audit of the top 20 Vietnamese universities' AI integrity policies as a contribution to the international literature.

nguon_viet_nam: Bretag's 5 Core Elements framework has not been applied in published Vietnamese academic integrity research as of early 2026 [uncertain]. However, the framework is directly relevant to MOET's ongoing policy development: Vietnamese universities typically have Decree 109 compliance on paper (Access + Detail) but lack the educative Approach and student Support elements. A Vietnamese translation of Bretag et al. (2011) and application to MOET policy would be a high-value research contribution.
